Official documentation for HabitForge, a habit tracker that draws your consistency as a rope: it thickens with what you keep and frays where you stopped.
HabitForge on Android is a native app with over-the-air updates, so fixes reach you without a store release. Install it from Google Play.
HabitForge is a PWA — install it to your home screen from any browser and keep checking in offline. Check-ins made without a connection sync when you reconnect.
Achievements are milestones HabitForge unlocks as you build habits — streaks, points, and consistency goals — each with a celebration moment and bonus points.
HabitForge drafts a habit's loop, reads your week back, helps word a post, and turns what you say into suggested check-ins, habits and posts. Nothing is saved until you press Save.
HabitForge's analytics turn your check-in history into weekly charts, so you can see which habits are holding and where consistency is slipping.
HabitForge's community adds a board, challenges, friends and a leaderboard, with report and block tools. A new profile is visible by default; you can change it.
An in-app bell tells you what happened while you were away, and your own device raises the reminders: one a day, and one per habit on the days it is due.
HabitForge ships light and dark themes plus a customiser for appearance, accent colour, radius, scaling and font size. Your choices follow your account.
Every main HabitForge page has a short tour behind the signpost button in the header, and the How HabitForge works page explains the whole app in six steps.

Edit a habit's details, pause it while you are away, or delete it for good. Pausing keeps your history; deleting removes the habit permanently.

HabitForge is a habit tracker that draws your consistency as a rope you can see. A new habit is a thread. Keep showing up and it thickens through string, rope and cable towards a chain; stop, and it frays where you stopped, while the rest of what you built stays. It runs as a web app and as an Android app on Google Play. There is no iOS build and no browser extension.

New here? Get started covers opening the app and signing in. Building your first habit? Create a habit walks through the form, then check-ins and streaks. Curious about the rope? Rope strength explains the meter.

Track habits you want to build, break or maintain, around the cue → routine → reward loop. Check in daily for streaks and points, and climb ten levels from Spark to Forge Master. Watch the rope — each habit's strength, from your current streak (40 per cent), your habits' average (30 per cent) and today's progress (30 per cent). Read your week in analytics, unlock achievements, and join the community. Make it yours with ten appearance settings, dark mode included, that follow your account. Keep tracking offline — the web app is a PWA that queues check-ins without a connection.

Open the app: habitforge.aoneahsan.com Docs source: github.com/aoneahsan/habitforge-docs Built by: the HabitForge team, at aoneahsan@gmail.com The app source is private; these docs are public. There is a free tier, plus Pro and Family plans; pricing lists what each covers.

The HabitForge Android app is on Google Play: install it from its store page. This page describes what the native app adds. The web app works on Android too: it installs to the home screen and works offline — see Install and offline. There is no iOS app yet, because it needs an Apple Developer account. On iPhone or iPad, use the web app and add it to your home screen.

The Android app updates itself in the background. When a fix or improvement ships, the app fetches it and applies it, so you get updates without waiting for a full store release. You keep using HabitForge normally while updates arrive.

Push notifications are optional and off unless you turn them on. When enabled, HabitForge can send you the occasional announcement. Your daily and per-habit reminders are separate: they are raised by your own device and arrive whether or not push is on. On Android 13 and newer, the app asks for notification permission the first time you opt in — never at launch.
Sign-in on Android is Google-only, using the device's native account picker. See Get started.

Use the web app on your phone in the meantime — add it to your home screen and it behaves like an installed app. Enable notifications only if you want them — the rope works fine as a silent cue. Your data follows your Google account, so the Android app and the web app stay in sync.
Install and offline — the web/PWA install path. Get started — sign in and add a habit. Changelog — what each release added.
HabitForge is a Progressive Web App (PWA), so you can install it to your home screen and keep tracking without a connection. No app store is required for the web version — the browser installs it.

Desktop (Chrome, Edge): use the install icon in the address bar, or the browser menu's "Install HabitForge". Android: the browser offers "Add to Home screen". The native app is on Google Play as well. iPhone / iPad: in Safari, tap Share → Add to Home Screen. This is how iOS users run HabitForge, since there is no App Store build. Once installed, HabitForge opens in its own window like any other app.

HabitForge keeps working when you lose connectivity: Your habits and recent data are cached on the device. Check-ins you make offline are queued and sync automatically when you reconnect. The header shows when you are offline so you know changes are pending. Because sync is automatic, you rarely have to think about it — track as usual and HabitForge reconciles when the network returns.
Install it so a home-screen tap is all it takes to check in. Trust the queue. Offline check-ins are not lost; they sync later. On iOS, add to home screen for a full-window, app-like experience.
The Android app — what the native build adds, once it ships. Get started — open the app and sign in. Themes and customiser — set your look once, keep it everywhere.

Achievements are milestones HabitForge unlocks as you keep going. Reaching a streak length, a points total, or a consistency goal unlocks an achievement, complete with a celebration moment and bonus points.

As you check in, HabitForge watches for milestones in the background. When you hit one, the achievement unlocks — with a short celebration naming the points it earned. Bonus points are added to your total, which can raise your level. Unlocked achievements are collected on your achievements page, where you can share one. You do not opt in or configure anything — achievements appear as you earn them.

Consistency unlocks the most. Many achievements are about showing up repeatedly, not doing anything extra. Share a milestone. The share button sends an achievement to another app, or copies a link to it. Let them be a surprise. You do not need to chase achievements — they follow good habits.
Levels and points — where the bonus points go. Community — share achievements with friends. Analytics — the trends that lead to milestones.

Four features use AI, each sending Anthropic — or OpenAI, when our Anthropic credit is used up — only what that request needs. An AI draft can be wrong. Nothing reaches your habits, check-ins or the community until you press Save or Post.

Habit drafts. On a new habit, Draft with AI fills the cue, routine, reward, craving and investment from the habit's name. Put back what I had restores what you wrote. Weekly reflections. The dashboard reads your last seven finished days back, habit by habit, with one suggestion. Post wording. On the community board, Help me word this rewords a post you wrote. It never writes one from nothing. Speak. Speak listens to what you did and what you want to start, then suggests records for you to check.

One recording can suggest three kinds of record: check-ins for habits you did today or yesterday, a new habit with its cue, routine and reward, and a community post. Nothing is saved until you press Save. Change or skip any suggestion first.
Press Speak, then Start recording. The microphone is asked for only then. Recordings run up to 2 minutes.

The AI levels. Spark is on Free. Pulse is on Pro. Surge is on Family, and on Pro after three unbroken paid months. Settings → AI shows your level and this month's use, which comes back on the 1st. The allowance for each feature is on the plans page.

documents.t: Settings → Your recordings: play, read or delete. The audio is deleted after 30 days; the words and suggestions stay until you delete the recording or your account. Who processes what, and the full detail, is in the privacy policy.
documents.s: Where do my recordings go, and for how long?

documents.t: Analytics turn your check-in history into a weekly picture of how your habits are doing. Instead of a single number, you get charts that show the shape of your consistency over time.

Weekly summaries of check-ins across your habits. Trends that make a slipping habit visible before the rope frays. Per-habit history so you can tell which habits are holding and which need attention. Charts are drawn with D3 and read directly from your own check-in data — nothing is estimated or inferred about you.

Look weekly, act daily. The weekly view spots patterns; the daily check-in fixes them. Compare habits. If one habit is dragging, its trend line usually shows it first. Use it after a slip. Analytics make it obvious when a habit is recovering.
Check-ins and streaks — the data behind the charts. Rope strength — the same story, drawn as a rope. Achievements — milestones worth celebrating.

The community is the side of HabitForge for people who track better together. You can use HabitForge entirely on your own, and nothing makes you post. Being seen, though, is on by default: a new profile is public and appears on the leaderboard until you change it. Both controls are in Settings and are described below.

Board — post updates, like and comment, and delete your own posts. The app calls this the board. Challenges — create or join a shared goal over a set window. Every participant's check-ins are scored against the target, standings update as people check in, and when the window closes the challenge names a winner. If several people tie, they all win — no tie-breaker invents a difference the challenge never measured. Friends — send and accept friend requests to build your circle. Leaderboard — see where you stand by points, with your level badge. Opting out hides you from everyone else's board, and you can still see your own rank.

Some challenges are tied to a habit rather than to check-ins in general. When you join one of those you pick which of your own habits it scores — so the same challenge can measure a run for one person and a page of reading for another. If you later delete the habit you picked, your score freezes where it was rather than quietly reopening.

Community features include moderation you control: Report any post or comment you think breaks the rules. Block a user to remove them from your board, comments, search, leaderboard, requests, and notifications. Blocking also ends any friendship. You choose your profile visibility and can take yourself off the leaderboard in Settings. Both start switched on, so this is a choice you make rather than one you are asked for: a new profile is public and ranked until you change it.

Join one challenge, not ten. A single shared goal is easier to sustain. Set your visibility first. Decide what you want public before you post. Use block freely. It is a personal filter — the other person is not notified.
Achievements — milestones worth sharing. Levels and points — what the leaderboard ranks. Privacy and terms — how community data is handled.
HabitForge has two separate things that tell you something: a bell inside the app, and reminders your device raises on its own. Both are yours to turn off.

The bell in the header collects what happened while you were away — an achievement you unlocked, a friend request, a comment on your post, a challenge you joined starting or finishing. Opening it marks what you have read, and the count clears. Nothing in the bell is sent to you by email or push. It waits until you come back.

Turn on Daily reminders in Settings and pick a time. Once a day, at that time, your device raises a notification nudging you to check in. Two things worth knowing: It comes from your device, not from our servers. Your phone schedules it locally, so it arrives whether or not you have a connection, and no reminder times leave your device. One switch covers both channels. There is no separate "push" toggle to find. Turning the switch on asks your device for notification permission the first time — never at launch, and never before you ask for it. If you deny permission, or turn notifications off for HabitForge at the operating-system level, the switch turns itself back off rather than promising something it cannot deliver.

Each habit can carry its own reminder. Open the habit, switch on Remind me about this habit and pick a time; the nudge arrives at that time on the days that habit is actually due — every day for a daily habit, weekdays only for a weekday one, and just the days you picked for anything else. It is titled with the habit's own name, so a glance at the lock screen tells you what it is for. Pausing the habit stops it. A paused habit is not due, and nudging you about something the app itself has stopped counting would be worse than silence. The same switch governs it. Turning Daily reminders off in Settings turns every per-habit reminder off too — there is no second place to look. One nudge a day at most, per habit, and turning any of them off never affects your streak.
HabitForge sends very little email: a welcome message, the occasional achievement, and a weekly digest carrying your own week. There are no marketing emails.

The bell cannot be turned off, but it never interrupts you — it only fills in. Reminders — the daily one and every per-habit one — are off until you turn them on, and the one switch in Settings turns them all back off. Email preferences live in Settings alongside the reminder.
Achievements — most of what the bell announces. Themes and customiser — including a Sound setting for in-app cues. Privacy and terms — what is collected and why.

HabitForge lets you shape how the app looks across nine separate settings, from a light/dark switch to the shape of a corner. Open the customiser from the palette icon in the header — it is on every page, at every width, and it works whether or not you are signed in.

Setting What it changes Appearance Light, Dark, or follow your system. Colour Ember, Quench, or Indigo — the accent used by buttons, highlights, and the active navigation. Corners Square, Soft, Rounded, or Full. Density How much breathing room sits between things. Text size Scales the type without breaking the layout. Typeface The font the app is set in. Panels How cards and panels are treated. Motion Animation, including turning it off. Your system's "reduce motion" setting is respected on its own. Sound Short cues on a few actions, off by default. Selections use visual card previews rather than dropdowns, so you can see each option before you choose it. A Reset to defaults option restores the original look.

Signed out: preferences save on your device, so the app reopens the way you left it. Signed in: preferences also sync to your account, so the same look follows you to another device. Your choice is applied before the first paint, so you never see a flash of the wrong theme while the page loads.
Analytics — read your week. Install and offline — keep your look on an installed copy.

HabitForge shows you around in two ways: a short tour of the page you are on, and one page that explains the whole app in six steps. Both are there whenever you want them, and neither starts by itself.
documents.s: Page tours and How HabitForge works

documents.t: Nine pages have a tour: the landing page, Today, Habits, New habit, Analytics, Achievements, Community, Settings and Plans. Start it from the signpost button, Take a tour of this page. It sits beside the theme button in the header, on every page that has a tour, on a phone too. The first time you open one of those pages, a short line under the button says New here? Take a quick tour of this page. It shows once per page, and once for your account, so a second device does not repeat it. It leaves by itself after a few seconds. Move through it with Back and Next. All steps lets you jump to any step, and Skip tour or Escape closes it at any point. Share a step. The address carries the step (?tour=3), so a link opens the tour at that step. On a phone the step card sits at the bottom of the screen, and the part of the page it explains is scrolled into view.

How HabitForge works is the whole app in six steps, one real screen each: Create a habit: name it, pick build, break or maintain, and write the loop. Check in each day: one press on Today, and press it again to undo. Watch the rope thicken: thread, string, rope, cable, chain. Keep going with other people: the board, friends, challenges and the leaderboard. Say it with Speak: say what you did, and nothing is saved until you press Save. Pick a plan when you need one: Free is the whole product; Pro and Family lift the ceilings. It is open to everyone, signed in or not. Find it under How it works in the sidebar's foot, in the site footer, and on the sitemap. The address carries the step too (?step=3), and the arrow keys and a swipe move between steps.
Getting started with HabitForge takes two steps: open the app, then sign in with Google. There is no separate account to create and no password to remember.

On the web: go to habitforge.aoneahsan.com in any modern browser. It works on desktop and mobile. On Android: install HabitForge from Google Play, or open the web app in Chrome and add it to your home screen — it installs and works offline. See The Android app for what the native app adds. There is no iOS app yet. On an iPhone or iPad, use the web app in Safari and add it to your home screen.

HabitForge uses Google sign-in only. On the web this is a Google popup; on Android it uses the native account picker. There is no email-and-password option, no Apple sign-in, and no anonymous mode. Click Continue with Google. Pick the Google account you want to use. You land on the dashboard, ready to add a habit. Your habits, streaks and settings sync to that Google account, so signing in on another device restores everything, down to the ten appearance settings you chose.
A habit is something you want to build, break or maintain. From the dashboard, give it a name and a schedule, then check in each day to start a streak. The full walkthrough is in Create a habit.

Start with one or two habits. Consistency compounds faster than a long list you cannot keep. Pick a real cue. "After my morning coffee" beats "sometime today" — the cue → routine → reward loop is what makes a habit stick. Check in honestly. The rope is only useful if it reflects what actually happened.
Create a habit Check-ins and streaks Levels and points
A check-in is how you tell HabitForge you did a habit. Each day a habit is due, you mark it done from the dashboard. Consecutive check-ins build a streak, and every check-in adds points.

Open the dashboard. Habits due today sit at the top with a check button. Tap the button to check in for that habit. Your streak for the habit goes up, points are added, and the rope grows a little stronger. Miss a due day and the streak resets — the rope starts to fray. Streaks count consecutive on-schedule days, so a habit scheduled for weekdays is not broken by skipping a weekend it was not due.

A broken streak resets the one you are running. It does not erase the longest one you have ever reached — that is kept separately and shown on your dashboard and on the leaderboard. It only ever goes up. Missing a day costs you the current run and nothing else, which is the point: the number that says what you are capable of should not be deleted by one bad week.
Check-ins earn points that accumulate across all your habits. Points raise your forge level through ten tiers — see Levels and points.

Check in at the same time each day. A fixed moment (right after your cue) makes the check-in itself a habit. Do not backfill dishonestly. The rope is only useful when it reflects what really happened. A reset is not a failure. Streaks are meant to restart; the level and total points you have earned stay with you.
Rope strength — the picture behind the streak. Levels and points — how points become a level. Analytics — your week at a glance.

A habit in HabitForge is something you want to build, break, or maintain, tracked on a schedule you choose. Creating one is a single form: give it a name and a schedule, and optionally describe the behaviour using the habit-loop fields.

Name — what the habit is, in plain words. "Drink water after waking" is clearer than "Be healthy". Category — used to group and colour your habits. Type — build a new habit, break an old one, or maintain one you already have. Schedule — how often the habit should happen (for example daily, or specific days of the week). That is enough to save. The habit appears on your dashboard, ready for its first check-in.

HabitForge is built around the cue → routine → reward loop from Charles Duhigg's The Power of Habit, extended with two more fields: Cue — the trigger. "After my morning coffee." Routine — the behaviour itself. Reward — what you get out of it, in your own words. Craving — why you want it. Investment — what you put in to make it stick. These fields are optional, but filling in a concrete cue and reward tends to keep a habit alive longer than the name alone.

Start small. Two habits done daily beat ten done once. Write the cue as an "after". Anchoring a habit to an existing routine gives it a reliable trigger. Phrase the reward as identity. "I am someone who finishes what they start" is more durable than "get fit".
Check-ins and streaks — how showing up builds a streak. Rope strength — what the strength meter shows. Manage habits — edit, pause, or delete.

Points are the total you build across every habit; your level is the tier those points put you in. Check-ins earn points, achievements add bonus points, and as your total grows you climb a ten-step forge ladder.

There are ten tiers, from your first check-in to a long-running practice: Level Tier 1 Spark 2 Kindling 3 Ember 4 Flame 5 Forge Hand 6 Apprentice Smith 7 Journeyman 8 Blacksmith 9 Master Smith 10 Forge Master Early tiers come quickly so progress feels real in the first week; later tiers widen so the top stays meaningful. Your points are the source of truth — every screen computes your level from them, so a level is simply the tier your current point total falls into.
A level tile on the dashboard shows your points, current tier, and progress to the next. A level badge appears on your profile and, if you join the community, on leaderboard rows.

Points reward consistency, not intensity. Many small check-ins outpace a single burst. Achievements are a shortcut. Unlocking one adds bonus points — see Achievements. The number is a nudge, not the goal. The rope tells you how a habit is doing; the level tells you how far you have come overall.
Check-ins and streaks — where points come from. Achievements — bonus points and celebration moments. Community — the leaderboard your level appears on.
Every habit has a menu for changing it after you create it: edit, pause, or delete. Open a habit's menu (the ⋮ button on its card) to choose one.
Change a habit's name, category, type, schedule, or any of the habit-loop fields. Edits apply going forward and do not rewrite your past check-ins.

Pausing takes a habit off your daily list without losing your history. Use it when a habit does not apply for a while — travel, illness, a season change. Its history and points stay intact, and you can resume it any time. A paused habit is not counted as missed while it is paused. Resuming does start the run again from zero, so a pause protects what you have already earned rather than the streak you were on.
Deleting removes the habit and its history permanently. This cannot be undone, so pause instead if you might return to the habit later.

Pause, do not delete, for a break. You keep the history and the points; the current run restarts when you resume. Edit the schedule rather than starting over. Changing days keeps the habit's history and rope. Delete to declutter. If a habit no longer fits your life, removing it keeps your dashboard focused.
Create a habit — the fields you are editing. Check-ins and streaks — what a pause keeps, and what it does not. Account and data — deleting your whole account.

The rope is HabitForge's way of showing how strong a habit is. A brand-new habit is a thin thread; as you keep checking in, it thickens towards a chain. Slip, and it starts to fray. The rope is drawn with D3 and updates as you check in.

The rope's strength is a deterministic, client-side calculation — not a machine-learning model and not a prediction. It combines three things: Current streak, 40 per cent — how many on-schedule days in a row. Average across your habits, 30 per cent — how the rest of your habits are running. Done today, 30 per cent — how much of today you have already completed. Because it is deterministic, the same inputs always produce the same rope. There is no hidden scoring and nothing is guessed about you.

The rope moves through stages as it strengthens — roughly thread → string → rope → cable → chain. A thin, frayed strand means a habit that is new or recently interrupted; a thick, solid one means a habit you have held for a long time.

Watch the trend, not the day. One missed day frays the rope a little; a pattern of misses is what thins it. Let the visual be the reminder. For many habits the rope is a stronger cue than a notification. Rebuild beats restart. After a slip, a few honest check-ins visibly repair the rope.
Check-ins and streaks — what feeds the rope. Levels and points — the account-wide counterpart. Analytics — the numbers behind the picture.
What is new in HabitForge, latest first. These notes mirror the app's release notes, so what you read here matches what shipped.

Plans are paid for by card on the plans page; the other way to pay is gone. The privacy policy now names OpenAI, which writes the AI drafts when our Anthropic credit is used up. A keyboard shows where it is on every control again, the help page speaks for the HabitForge team, and the feed lists the latest releases. The Android app is on Google Play, and these pages now say so. The appearance panel lists nine choices: the pointer is the browser's own again.

documents.t: Pro and Family can now be paid for by card on the plans page. The card is entered on a page run by Polar, the payment provider; the app never sees it. The plan starts when the payment is confirmed, usually within a minute, and the same page shows the subscription with its renewal date, a way to cancel or resume it, and, for Family, a way to change the number of seats. Paying another way still works and is still granted by hand. Web only: the Android app sells nothing.
documents.s: Web — 2026-10-02 — pay for a plan by card

documents.t: Every member now has a link. When somebody creates an account from it and verifies their email, the member earns points and a badge, and a plan month once enough people have joined — the numbers are set from the admin's own screen rather than fixed in the app. The page shows a count and a state, never who joined, and it produces a link and nothing else. The person who accepts an invitation is told so on the sign-up page, and is never named to the inviter.

documents.t: Two small panels now show one of the developer's own other apps: on today's entry and under the community board. No advertising network is involved, HabitForge never promotes itself, and the words are edited from the admin's own screen. Sharing the pricing page now produces a card that names the plans. Web only: the Android build of that day was unchanged, and its store answer for ads stays "No" until a build carries the panels.

documents.t: About the numbering The versions listed below this one — 1.2.0, 1.1.0 and 1.0 — are the development history of the earlier app this one replaced. None of them was ever published, so no one is being asked to move backwards: this is the first HabitForge release to reach a store, and it starts the version line at 1.0.0. HabitForge was rebuilt from the ground up. Same idea, same rope, new foundations — a new stack, a new backend, and a lot of things the 1.x app could not do. Feature — Habits gain real schedules, and pauses that keep your history while the run starts again from zero on resume. Feature — Check-ins work offline. They queue on your device and sync when you reconnect. Feature — Challenges are scored. Participants are ranked against the target, ties are joint wins, and a challenge can be bound to a habit each person chooses for themselves. Feature — Plans, and a free tier that is genuinely generous. Free carries 30 habits, 30 challenges a month and up to 500 friends — the things that cost nothing to run are not the things worth rationing. Pro and a Family household whose members inherit the plan sit above it. See pricing, which reads its numbers from the live plan table rather than from a page somebody has to remember to update. Feature — A notification bell for what happened while you were away. Feature — Reminders raised by your own device. A daily one at a time you choose, and a reminder per habit, on the days that habit is actually due. Both are scheduled on your phone rather than sent from a server, so they are right across a time-zone change and work with no connection at all. Feature — A third kind of habit: Maintain, beside Build and Break — for the things you are keeping up rather than starting or stopping. Feature — Your longest streak ever, on the dashboard and on the leaderboard, kept separately from the one you are running now so a broken streak no longer erases what you did. Feature — A line on your dashboard about the people you know — who kept what today. Feature — Export everything you have, or delete your account, from inside the app. Improvement — The theme customiser grows from a handful of options to ten settings, applied before the first paint so there is no flash of the wrong theme. Improvement — Every screen was rebuilt for keyboard and screen-reader use. Improvement — The household screens. If you own a Family plan you get a roster, a seat meter, an invitation list and a way to hand the household over; if you are a member you get a plain account of what you inherit and one way out. Improvement — Deleting your account now tells you it worked before signing you out, instead of the app simply disappearing. Improvement — Every link that leaves HabitForge opens in a new tab. Removed — Profile photos. Profiles now carry a handle and a display name. Android: the native app is built, signed and uploaded to Google Play for testing, the first step before the public track. The web app installs to your home screen in the meantime.

Feature — Upload a profile photo, shown on the leaderboard and community posts. Feature — In-app contact form on the Help page, so you do not need a mail app. Improvement — Automatic in-app updates so fixes arrive without waiting for a store update. Improvement — Faster startup and lighter pages through code-splitting and lazy loading. Improvement — Groundwork for more reliable error handling and analytics. Fixes — Data, reliability, and UI polish throughout.

Feature — Share your streaks, achievements, and the app with friends. Improvement — In-app Privacy, Terms, and Account-deletion pages. Improvement — Android App Links and a habitforge:// deep link, so shared links open straight in the app. Improvement — Brand and app-icon refresh. Fixes — Stability and polish.

Feature — Create and track habits with the cue, routine, and reward loop. Feature — Daily check-ins with streaks and points. Feature — Rope-strength visualisation that grows with your consistency. Feature — Weekly analytics and charts. Feature — Optional community: posts, comments, challenges, friends, and a leaderboard. Feature — Achievements with celebration moments. Feature — Light and dark themes with a theme customiser. Feature — Offline support so tracking works without a connection.
The Android app — where automatic updates land. Get started — try the latest release.
HabitForge's authoritative privacy policy and terms live in the app itself. This page summarises the essentials and links to the current, in-app versions.

Privacy policy: habitforge.aoneahsan.com/privacy Terms of service: habitforge.aoneahsan.com/terms Delete your account: habitforge.aoneahsan.com/delete-account The in-app pages are the source of truth. If anything here differs from them, follow the in-app versions.

Sign-in is Google-only. HabitForge uses your Google account to identify you; there is no password to store. Your data is your habits. Habits, check-ins, streaks, achievements, and community activity are stored so the app can show them back to you. Notifications are optional. Push is off until you turn it on. The community is opt-in. Nothing about you appears in the community unless you choose to participate, and you control your visibility.
Export your data from Settings. Delete your account from Settings or the delete-account page. Deletion removes your habits, check-ins, community posts, and profile. It cannot be undone.
Support — contact the author or report an issue. Community — report and block tools. Manage habits — pause or delete individual habits.
The quickest way to get help with HabitForge is the in-app contact form on the Help page. You can also reach the author directly or file a documentation issue.

In-app contact form — open the Help page in HabitForge and send a message. No mail app needed. Email — aoneahsan@gmail.com. Documentation issues — spotted a mistake on this site? Open one at github.com/aoneahsan/habitforge-docs/issues.

HabitForge is built and maintained by the HabitForge team. It has a free tier that is a real product rather than a trial, plus Pro and Family plans that lift its limits — see pricing. If it helps you and you want to give back, you can contribute here: aoneahsan.com/payment — support HabitForge A contribution is voluntary and separate from a plan; it unlocks nothing on its own.
